text: Nadia had not told anyone about the car, and by the third week the not-telling had become its own weight. The night of the wedding she had driven home from the reception with two glasses of wine in her and a headache behind her eyes. The rain was thin and the road was dark. She had felt the soft bump and told herself it was a bag, a branch, something from the verge. In the morning the local paper ran a short piece about a cyclist found in a drainage ditch, alive but badly hurt, and a description of a silver hatchback. Nadia read it at the kitchen table while her husband poured the coffee. She got up to refill her cup so he would not see her face. Every day since she had checked the front bumper for dents and found none, because she had already paid cash for repairs at a shop two towns away. She was not a bad person, she kept telling herself, and the guilty part of her did not believe it. The guilt sat under her ribs, heavy and steady. Each evening her husband asked about her day, and each evening she lied about one small thing to keep the big thing buried, and felt the lies pile up like wet leaves against a drain.

I need to get this out somewhere. Six years ago I was the supervisor who signed off on the layoffs at the plant. The list came from upstairs, but I picked the names for my floor and I didn't push back on a single one. Last month I ran into Greg Holt at the hardware store. He's driving for a delivery app now, his kid is at community college, and he asked how I was doing like we were old friends. I said fine and bought a box of screws I didn't need. I've felt guilty about it for years, the kind that wakes you at 4am running the names. I've never told my wife the full story. I've never apologized to him, because I'm scared it would sound like I want forgiveness for free. I don't know what I'm asking. Maybe whether anyone has made a real amends to someone they hurt at work, and whether it helped them or only helped the person saying sorry. Be honest. I can take it.

Dear Priya, I owe you an apology I should have made in March, and I'm sorry it's coming in a letter. I'm guilty of something I can't undo. I read your draft in the shared folder before you sent it to the committee, copied your analysis into my own slides, and presented it as mine. You were on leave with the baby, and I told Helen you were 'not able to commit to the timeline.' That was a lie. The promotion went to me. I have felt sick about it ever since, and the guilt has grown worse every time I hear your name in a meeting. I told myself I was protecting the team. That isn't true, and you deserve the real reason, which is that I wanted it and I took it. I've written to Helen to correct the record, and I'll sign whatever statement the committee needs. I'm not asking you to say it's fine. I just couldn't keep being the person who had done that and said nothing. Best, Tom.

Sunday. Called Mum back at last. She asked about the funeral flowers and I said I'd sorted them, which I hadn't. The card still sits in my jacket pocket, the one I never gave to Ruth at the hospital because I got there too late. Drove past the house on the way back from the shop. Lights off in the front room where Dad watched the football. I haven't been inside since. Lena texted a photo of the kids at the park and I sent back a thumbs up and then wanted to throw the phone in the river. Cooked dinner for one and left half of it in the pan. Went through the drawer of his old letters, the ones from the care home asking me to visit. Found my own handwriting on an envelope I'd addressed and never posted. Dated October. I sat on the bathroom floor for a while with my back against the tub. Then I got up and fixed the tap that has dripped since spring, because at least that is a thing I can put right.

The lawyer's office smelled of lemon polish and old carpet. Owen signed where the tabs said to sign and pushed the folder back across the desk. His brother's name was on the first page, and on the third page, in smaller type, was the sum withdrawn from the family account over four years, always on the first business day of the month. He had told himself he would put it back. He had told Caroline the same thing each time she asked why the statements looked thin. In the car afterward he sat with both hands on the wheel and did not turn the key. Across the lot a man in a tie was loading golf clubs into a trunk. Owen thought about his brother's kids, who had called him Uncle Owen at the funeral with their faces wet and trusting. He thought about the sealed envelope in the glovebox that held a handwritten list of dates. After a while he took out his phone and opened a message to his brother's widow, closed it, then opened it again and typed the first line before his hands could decide otherwise.
